newsitem.title: USA: U.S. does not see Iraq role in Kurdish fighting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. does not see Iraq role in Kurdish fighting.

text.p: The United States insisted on Sunday it would not let Iraqi President Saddam Hussein repress his ethnic minorities but said it lacked evidence of a major Iraqi role in fresh Kurdish factional fighting in northern Iraq.
Defense Secretary William Perry referred to inter-Kurdish fighting as a civil war in which it would be a mistake for the United States to intervene.

He said the United States did not know the scope of Iraqi involvement in the latest clashes between the Kurdish Democratic Party (PDK), which has invited Saddam's help, and the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

"My judgment is that we should not be involved in the civil war in the north," Perry said on the CBS program "Face the Nation." Instead, the United States should focus "where our interests are, which is not just in the south, it's the strategic heartland of Iraq." Iraq borders the oil-producing U.S. allies of Kuwait and Saudi Arabia to the south and southwest and Jordan to the west.

General John Shalikashvili, the top U.S. military officer, said Saddam appeared to have withdrawn all but several hundred of his troops from the allied-declared Kurdish safe haven set up after the 1991 Gulf War.

"Our judgment is that it's certainly in the hundreds and not in the thousands," Shalikashvili said of the number of Iraqi troops thought by the United States to remain in the zone supposedly off-limits to Iraqi onslaught.

Earlier in the day, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan claimed that Iraqi artillery and tanks had mowed down its defenses to let PDK forces take two major towns, Degala and Koi Sanjaq, that had been controlled by the PUK.

Decrying what it called an Iraqi onslaught, the PUK urged the United States and its allies to prevent further military moves by Saddam in what is supposed to be the protected area for Kurds north of the 36th parallel.

"Urgent and decisive help is needed," Barham Salih, a PUK spokesman in Washington, told Reuters. "This is an Iraqi onslaught on the Kurdish people. They must not be able to get away with using Kurdish mercenaries as a fig leaf."

Intervening in Iraqi Kurdistan is fraught with problems for Washington. The United States wants to maintain the territorial integrity of Iraq as a counterweight to the fundamentalist government in Iran, which Washington accuses of being the biggest sponsor of international terrorism.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the United States fired 44 cruise missiles at military targets in southern Iraq to punish Saddam for sending 40,000 or more of his troops into the Kurdish safe haven on Aug. 31 to take the town of Arbil.
U.S. leaders said on Sunday they would not stand idly by if Saddam's forces attacked the Kurds in the north or the Shiites in another protected zone in Iraq's south or moved against its neighbors.

"We will ensure, as we have in the past, that Saddam Hussein does not take action against his own people or against his neighbors that threatens their welfare and their security, just like we did a few days ago," Shalikashvili said on the NBC program "Meet the Press."
The United States was seeing "some indications" that Saddam might be trying to repair some air defense facilities disabled by the cruise missile strikes last week, he said.
"We have warned Saddam Hussein that any attempt to repair those sites or to reinforce them will be taken very seriously, and he must understand the consequences of such an act," Shalikashvili said.
After the cruise missile strikes last week, the United States widened a zone in the south where it prohibits Iraqi aircraft to fly, bringing it to the outskirts of Baghdad.

Senior U.S. officials said U.S. policy was to contain Saddam, whom they have branded a major threat to regional stability since he sent invasion forces into Kuwait in August 1990. Officials denied that the Gulf War coalition was unravelling because of opposition to the U.S. unilateral use of force against Iraq.

"It has been stated very clearly that the United States is leading and that there are times when we have to take action alone and our allies are with us," Madeleine Albright, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said on the ABC program "This Week with David Brinkley."
